3. Constructions🔗

In this chapter we will introduce some of the concrete examples of simple graphs that can be found in Mathlib together with a few new ones. The idea is to give a flavour of the kinds of constructions that are possible in Mathlib. It also offers a good excuse to introduce many of the fundamental types that may be unfamiliar to graph theorists but are used throughout Mathlib. These include Bool, Fin, Option, Prod, Sigma, Subtype, Sum and Unit. Another fundamental way of building types is the quotient of a type by an equivalence relation. We have already met one, Sym2 V (Edges); connected components are another (Connected Components); and much later we build our own for the blocks of a graph (Blocks As A Quotient Of Edges).

Two of the constructions we introduce below, the hypercube and Mycielskian, will serve as running examples throughout the remaining chapters.

Beware that in this chapter we are looking at constructions, and so we will see examples of complete bipartite graphs and cycle graphs etc., but we won't see any discussion yet of what it means for a graph to be bipartite or to contain a cycle etc.

To sanity-check our definitions, we will want to perform computations on small examples using #eval and decide. We will look at such computations in much more detail in the next chapter, but for them to work we need to provide decidability instances for adjacency in the graphs we define. Feel free to ignore these and revisit them once you have read the next chapter!

3.1. Basic Families of Graphs🔗

We start with the most basic families of graphs: complete and empty graphs, single edges, paths, cycles and complete bipartite graphs, as well as graphs defined by functions.

3.1.1. Complete and Empty Graphs🔗

Given a vertex set V the complete graph on V has all possible edges while the empty graph on V has no edges.

In Mathlib these are referred to by their roles as the top ⊤ and bottom ⊥ elements of the complete atomic Boolean algebra formed by SimpleGraph V (see Order for more details).

@[wikidata Q45715] abbrev completeGraph (V : Type u) : SimpleGraph V := ⊤#source completeGraph abbrev emptyGraph (V : Type u) : SimpleGraph V := ⊥#source emptyGraph

As we saw in Top And Bottom, results about these graphs use the top and bot names, as in top_adj and bot_adj.

Recall that Fin n is the type of natural numbers less than n with addition mod n. (In particular Fin 0 is the empty type.)

We can construct the complete graph on Fin n as follows.

example (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin n) := completeGraph (Fin n)

We can introduce the notation K[n] for the complete graph on Fin n as follows.

/-- The complete graph on Fin n is denoted K[n]. -/ scoped notation "K[" n "]" => completeGraph (Fin n)

Since Fin n has decidable equality, K[n] has decidable adjacency: if we have a procedure for deciding whether two vertices are equal then we can decide whether they are adjacent in the complete graph, since adjacency is simply not-equal-to ≠.

For example 10 and 111 are adjacent in K[417]

example : K[417].Adj 10 111 := V:Type u_1⊢ K[417].Adj 10 111 All goals completed! 🐙

We can similarly introduce the notation E[n] for the empty graph on Fin n.

/-- The empty graph on Fin n is denoted E[n]. -/ scoped notation "E[" n "]" => emptyGraph (Fin n)

3.1.2. A Single Edge🔗

We can construct a SimpleGraph V with just one edge between two vertices s : V and t : V using edge s t. If s = t then this is just the empty graph on V. (Recall that SimpleGraph V is a CompleteAtomicBooleanAlgebra: these graphs are the atoms of the algebra.)

def edge : SimpleGraph V := fromEdgeSet {s(s, t)}#source edge -- def edge : SimpleGraph V := fromEdgeSet {s(s, t)}

You may wonder why we care about the graph with a single edge, but in fact it can be very useful. Arguments about adding or removing a single edge to a graph can be formulated using it.

For example, if we add the edge s t to G, where s and t are distinct vertices that do not form an edge in G then we get a strictly larger graph.

SimpleGraph.lt_sup_edge.{u_1} {V : Type u_1} (G : SimpleGraph V) (s t : V) (hne : s ≠ t) (hn : ¬G.Adj s t) : G < G ⊔ edge s t#check lt_sup_edge -- .. (hne : s ≠ t) (hn : ¬G.Adj s t) : G < G ⊔ edge s t

3.1.3. Path Graphs🔗

In Mathlib the canonical path graph on n vertices is constructed as the Hasse diagram of the linear order on Fin n, so we first describe Hasse diagrams.

Given a poset (P, ≤) we say that a ∈ P is covered by b ∈ P if a < b and ∀ c ∈ P, a < c → ¬ c < b. In Mathlib this is denoted a ⋖ b.

The Hasse diagram of a poset (P, ≤) is the graph with vertex set P and edges between pairs of vertices such that one is covered by the other.

example {P : Type*} {u v : P} [PartialOrder P] : (hasse P).Adj u v ↔ u ⋖ v ∨ v ⋖ u := V:Type u_1P:Type u_2u:Pv:Pinst✝:PartialOrder P⊢ (hasse P).Adj u v ↔ u ⋖ v ∨ v ⋖ u All goals completed! 🐙

The path graph on n vertices is then the Hasse diagram of Fin n. Recall that addition in Fin n is defined mod n.

0#eval (2 : Fin 4) + 2 -- 0

So when describing adjacency in this graph we need to use the underlying ℕ values.

def pathGraph (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin n) := hasse _#source pathGraph example (n : ℕ) (a b : Fin n) : (pathGraph n).Adj a b ↔ a.val + 1 = b.val ∨ b.val + 1 = a.val := pathGraph_adj

We introduce the notation P[n] for path graphs as follows:

@[inherit_doc pathGraph] scoped notation "P[" n "]" => pathGraph n

Mathlib has no decidability instance for adjacency in hasse or pathGraph, so we will need to provide our own if we want to do computations with these graphs. This is a bit more work than the instances we give in this chapter, so we defer it until Decidability, Finiteness and Degrees.

3.1.4. Cycle Graphs🔗

For any n : ℕ we can define the cycle graph on n vertices as the graph with vertex set Fin n and edges between vertices that differ by 1 modulo n. Although we usually think of cycles as always containing at least 3 vertices, in Mathlib we also have cycle graphs on 0, 1, and 2 vertices. This is a common pattern in Mathlib: rather than add side conditions to the definition, we will instead need to check when using cycleGraph whether or not it is in fact a cycle!

For 3 ≤ n the definition of adjacency is obvious: Adj a b := a - b = 1 ∨ b - a = 1. This also makes sense for n = 2 but gives us the graph on Fin 2 with a single edge.

The cases n = 0 and n = 1 need a bit more care: for a b : Fin 0 we can't write a - b = 1 ∨ b - a = 1 since there is no 1 : Fin 0. While for a b : Fin 1 we can write a - b = 1 ∨ b - a = 1 but 1 = 0 in Fin 1 so this would define a graph with loops, which is not allowed.

example : (1 : Fin 1) = 0 := rfl

The solution is to define cycleGraph n to be the empty graph for n = 0 and n = 1.

def cycleGraph : (n : ℕ) → SimpleGraph (Fin n) | 0 | 1 => ⊥ | _ + 2 => { Adj a b := a - b = 1 ∨ b - a = 1 }#source cycleGraph -- def cycleGraph : (n : ℕ) → SimpleGraph (Fin n) -- | 0 | 1 => ⊥ -- | _ + 2 => { -- Adj a b := a - b = 1 ∨ b - a = 1 -- }

We introduce the notation C[n] for cycle graphs as follows:

@[inherit_doc cycleGraph] scoped notation "C[" n "]" => cycleGraph n C[5] : SimpleGraph (Fin 5)#check C[5] -- C[5] : SimpleGraph (Fin 5) example : C[5].Adj 0 1 := V:Type u_1⊢ C[5].Adj 0 1 All goals completed! 🐙 example : ¬ C[5].Adj 4 2 := V:Type u_1⊢ ¬C[5].Adj 4 2 All goals completed! 🐙

For n = 0 and n = 1, C[n] is the empty graph on Fin n, while for n = 2 it is K[2]. The first two of these are definitional equalities (in the sense of Definitional And Propositional Equalities), while the last is not. (C[2].Adj a b is a - b = 1 ∨ b - a = 1 while K[2].Adj a b is a ≠ b. We can prove that these are equivalent, but they are not definitionally equal.)

example : C[0] = E[0] := rfl example : C[1] = E[1] := rfl example : C[2] = K[2] := cycleGraph_two_eq_top

3.1.5. Complete Bipartite Graphs🔗

Given two disjoint vertex sets V and W we can form the complete bipartite graph with classes V and W. This seems to involve the idea that V and W are disjoint, but in Lean we are working with types not sets and so have no way of talking about disjointness of two arbitrary types.

Lean does however have the very useful Sum type, written V ⊕ W, which plays the role of the disjoint union of types V and W. Note that this is not the same as the set-theoretic union: any x : V ⊕ W "knows" which of the two sides of the sum it came from. It is either Sum.inl v, for some v : V or Sum.inr w for some w : W. (In particular we can form the disjoint union of a type with itself as V ⊕ V.)

@[suggest_for Either] inductive Sum (α : Type u) (β : Type v) where /-- Left injection into the sum type `α ⊕ β`. -/ | inl (val : α) : Sum α β /-- Right injection into the sum type `α ⊕ β`. -/ | inr (val : β) : Sum α β#source Sum V ⊕ V : Type u_1#check V ⊕ V

This gives a natural way to define complete bipartite graphs.

@[simps] def completeBipartiteGraph (V W : Type*) : SimpleGraph (V ⊕ W) where Adj v w := v.isLeft ∧ w.isRight ∨ v.isRight ∧ w.isLeft#source completeBipartiteGraph

We introduce the notation K[s, t] for the canonical complete bipartite graph with parts Fin s and Fin t as follows.

/-- The complete bipartite graph on Fin s ⊕ Fin t is denoted K[s, t]. -/ scoped notation "K[" s ", " t "]" => completeBipartiteGraph (Fin s) (Fin t) K[4, 5] : SimpleGraph (Fin 4 ⊕ Fin 5)#check K[4, 5] -- K[4, 5] : SimpleGraph (Fin 4 ⊕ Fin 5)

If we try to check adjacency of two vertices in K[4, 5] we get an error.The actual error is suppressed in the Lean source file by the #guard_msgs command and only shown in the HTML version. Delete the #guard_msgs line to see the error message in VSCode.

/- error: failed to synthesize Decidable (K[4, 5].Adj (Sum.inl 0) (Sum.inr 3)) -/ failed to synthesize Decidable (K[4, 5].Adj (Sum.inl 0) (Sum.inr 3)) Hint: Additional diagnostic information may be available using the `set_option diagnostics true` command.#eval K[4, 5].Adj (Sum.inl 0) (Sum.inr 3)

This is because, as for pathGraph, there is no decidability instance for completeBipartiteGraph in Mathlib. This time, though, it is easy to provide the missing instance ourselves. (Don't worry if this is unfamiliar, we will look at decidability in much more detail in Decidability, Finiteness and Degrees.)

instance (V W : Type*) : DecidableRel (completeBipartiteGraph V W).Adj := fun v w => V✝:Type u_1V:Type u_2W:Type u_3v:V ⊕ Ww:V ⊕ W⊢ Decidable ((completeBipartiteGraph V W).Adj v w) V✝:Type u_1V:Type u_2W:Type u_3v:V ⊕ Ww:V ⊕ W⊢ Decidable ({ Adj := fun v w ↦ v.isLeft = true ∧ w.isRight = true ∨ v.isRight = true ∧ w.isLeft = true, symm := ⋯, loopless := ⋯ }.Adj v w) All goals completed! 🐙 example : K[4, 5].Adj (Sum.inl 0) (Sum.inr 3) := V:Type u_1⊢ K[4, 5].Adj (Sum.inl 0) (Sum.inr 3) All goals completed! 🐙

3.2. Algebraic Constructions🔗

Next we look at two families of graphs whose vertices are the elements of a group, with adjacency defined using the group operation.

3.2.1. Circulant Graphs🔗

If G is an additive group and s ⊆ G, the associated circulant graph has vertex set G with edges between vertices whose difference belongs to s (suitably symmetrized so that the resulting graph is undirected and without loops).

@[simps!] def circulantGraph {G : Type*} [AddGroup G] (s : Set G) : SimpleGraph G := fromRel (· - · ∈ s)#source circulantGraph -- def circulantGraph {G : Type*} [AddGroup G] (s : Set G) : -- SimpleGraph G := fromRel (· - · ∈ s) example : SimpleGraph (Fin 8) := circulantGraph ({1, 3} : Set (Fin 8))

3.2.1.1. Paley Graphs🔗

A special case of a circulant graph is the Paley graph. If F is a finite field, the Paley graph of F is the circulant graph on F whose differences are the nonzero squares in F. Usually one also requires |F| ≡ 1 mod 4: then -1 is a square, so u - v is a square if and only if v - u is, and each vertex is adjacent to exactly half of the others. (For any other finite field the definition below gives the complete graph: if |F| ≡ 3 mod 4 then exactly one of d and -d is a square for each d ≠ 0, while if |F| is even then every element of F is a square.) The circulantGraph calls the constructor fromRel (· - · ∈ s), which automatically removes loops and symmetrizes the relation, so we can simply take all the squares, including 0.

/-- The Paley graph of a field F: distinct elements are adjacent if their difference is a square. -/ abbrev paleyGraph (F : Type*) [Field F] : SimpleGraph F := circulantGraph {y | IsSquare y}

Mathlib's type of integers modulo n is ZMod n. (For n ≠ 0 it is defined to be Fin n.) If p is prime then ZMod p is a field, so paleyGraph (ZMod p) is the Paley graph on p vertices. However, Lean will only find the Field (ZMod p) instance if it can find a proof that p is prime, in the form of an instance of Fact (Nat.Prime p). Mathlib provides these for p = 2 and p = 3, but for p = 17 we need to supply one ourselves.

instance fact_prime_seventeen : Fact (Nat.Prime 17) := ⟨V:Type u_1⊢ Nat.Prime 17 All goals completed! 🐙⟩ @[to_additive_dont_translate] def ZMod : ℕ → Type | 0 => ℤ | n + 1 => Fin (n + 1)#source ZMod example : SimpleGraph (ZMod 17) := paleyGraph (ZMod 17)

3.2.2. Cayley Graphs🔗

Cayley graphs are also defined in Mathlib. They are defined for any vertex type with a multiplication or addition operation, not just for groups.

If you look at the definition you will see the use of the @[to_additive] attribute to give both multiplicative and additive versions of the same construction. (In particular if you look for the source code for addCayley, you will be taken to mulCayley.)

@[to_additive /-- The Cayley graph induced by an operation `[Add M]` with generators `s` -/] def mulCayley {M : Type*} (s : Set M) [Mul M] : SimpleGraph M := fromRel (∃ g ∈ s, · * g = ·)#source mulCayley

The symmetric group on four points is Equiv.Perm (Fin 4) in Mathlib, and its elements can be written in cycle notation using c[...]. Taking a 3-cycle and a 4-cycle as generators gives the graph drawn below.

/-- The Cayley graph of the symmetric group on Fin 4 generated by a 3-cycle and a 4-cycle. -/ abbrev cayleyS4 : SimpleGraph (Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) := mulCayley {c[0, 1, 2], c[0, 1, 2, 3]}

It has one vertex for each of the 24 permutations and is 4-regular, since each generator accounts for two of the edges at every vertex: one to the neighbour it multiplies to, and one back from its inverse.

24#eval Fintype.card (Equiv.Perm (Fin 4)) -- 24 4#eval cayleyS4.degree 1 -- 4 48#eval cayleyS4.edgeFinset.card -- 48

The two edge colours in the figure are the two generators: the triangles are the edges contributed by the 3-cycle and the squares those contributed by the 4-cycle. Splitting the graph up like this is exactly mulCayley_union, which says that a union of generating sets gives the union of the corresponding Cayley graphs.

example : cayleyS4 = mulCayley {c[0, 1, 2]} ⊔ mulCayley {c[0, 1, 2, 3]} := V:Type u_1⊢ cayleyS4 = mulCayley {(↑[0, 1, 2]).formPerm ⋯} ⊔ mulCayley {(↑[0, 1, 2, 3]).formPerm ⋯} All goals completed! 🐙

3.3. Operations on Graphs🔗

So far each construction has built a graph from scratch. We now look at some ways of building new graphs from old ones.

3.3.1. Line Graphs🔗

Given G: SimpleGraph V, its line graph is the graph whose vertices are the edges of G, in which two distinct edges are adjacent iff they share a vertex. In Mathlib this is defined as follows.

def lineGraph : SimpleGraph G.edgeSet where Adj e₁ e₂ := e₁ ≠ e₂ ∧ (e₁ ∩ e₂ : Set V).Nonempty symm.symm e₁ e₂ hadj := by rwa [ne_comm, Set.inter_comm]#source lineGraph -- def lineGraph : SimpleGraph G.edgeSet where -- Adj e₁ e₂ := e₁ ≠ e₂ ∧ (e₁ ∩ e₂ : Set V).Nonempty -- symm.symm e₁ e₂ hadj := by rwa [ne_comm, Set.inter_comm]

We introduce the notation L[G] for the line graph of G as follows.

@[inherit_doc lineGraph] scoped notation "L[" G "]" => lineGraph G

The edge set G.edgeSet is a Set (Sym2 V), so to use it as the vertex type of L[G], Lean coerces it to the subtype {e : Sym2 V // e ∈ G.edgeSet}, written ↑G.edgeSet. A vertex of L[G] is therefore an edge bundled with a proof that it belongs to G: a term ⟨s(u, v), h⟩ with h : s(u, v) ∈ G.edgeSet. As we saw in Edges, this membership is the same as G.Adj u v. For a concrete graph, decide can supply h.

L[K[4]] : SimpleGraph ↑K[4].edgeSet#check L[K[4]] -- SimpleGraph ↑K[4].edgeSet ⟨s(0, 1), ⋯⟩ : { x // x ∈ K[4].edgeSet }#check (⟨s(0, 1), V:Type u_1⊢ s(0, 1) ∈ K[4].edgeSet All goals completed! 🐙⟩ : K[4].edgeSet)

Adjacency in L[G] has two parts. The condition e₁ ≠ e₂ is needed because every edge shares a vertex with itself, and simple graphs have no loops. The condition (e₁ ∩ e₂ : Set V).Nonempty says that the edges share a vertex. To state it, each edge is coerced twice: first from ↑G.edgeSet to Sym2 V, forgetting the proof of membership, and then from Sym2 V to Set V, the set of its endpoints.

For example, s(0, 1) and s(0, 2) are adjacent in L[K[4]]. After constructor, the first goal says that they are distinct and the second that they share a vertex, for which 0 is a witness.

example : L[K[4]].Adj ⟨s(0, 1), V:Type u_1⊢ s(0, 1) ∈ K[4].edgeSet All goals completed! 🐙⟩ ⟨s(0, 2), V:Type u_1⊢ s(0, 2) ∈ K[4].edgeSet All goals completed! 🐙⟩ := V:Type u_1⊢ L[K[4]].Adj ⟨s(0, 1), ⋯⟩ ⟨s(0, 2), ⋯⟩ V:Type u_1⊢ ⟨s(0, 1), ⋯⟩ ≠ ⟨s(0, 2), ⋯⟩V:Type u_1⊢ (↑↑⟨s(0, 1), ⋯⟩ ∩ ↑↑⟨s(0, 2), ⋯⟩).Nonempty V:Type u_1⊢ ⟨s(0, 1), ⋯⟩ ≠ ⟨s(0, 2), ⋯⟩ All goals completed! 🐙 V:Type u_1⊢ (↑↑⟨s(0, 1), ⋯⟩ ∩ ↑↑⟨s(0, 2), ⋯⟩).Nonempty V:Type u_1⊢ 0 ∈ ↑↑⟨s(0, 1), ⋯⟩ ∩ ↑↑⟨s(0, 2), ⋯⟩; All goals completed! 🐙

3.3.2. Box Products🔗

The box product of two graphs G and H is the graph on the Cartesian product of their vertex sets, where a pair of vertices (g₁, h₁) and (g₂, h₂) are adjacent if either g₁ = g₂ and H.Adj h₁ h₂ or h₁ = h₂ and G.Adj g₁ g₂. This is written G □ H in Mathlib. Its vertex type is the product type V × W, whose elements are pairs (g, h); for x : V × W the two components are x.1 and x.2 (also written x.fst and x.snd).

def boxProd (G : SimpleGraph α) (H : SimpleGraph β) : SimpleGraph (α × β) where Adj x y := G.Adj x.1 y.1 ∧ x.2 = y.2 ∨ H.Adj x.2 y.2 ∧ x.1 = y.1 symm.symm x y := by simp [eq_comm, adj_comm]#source boxProd

Adjacency in the box product of a path and a cycle. (We use n + 2 because Mathlib's cycleGraph_adj is stated for cycleGraph (n + 2); the more awkward cycleGraph_adj' covers every n.)

example {n : ℕ} {a b c d : Fin (n + 2)} : (P[n + 2] □ C[n + 2]).Adj (a, b) (c, d) ↔ ((a.val + 1 = c.val ∨ c.val + 1 = a.val) ∧ b = d) ∨ ((b - d = 1 ∨ d - b = 1) ∧ a = c) := V:Type u_1n:ℕa:Fin (n + 2)b:Fin (n + 2)c:Fin (n + 2)d:Fin (n + 2)⊢ (P[n + 2] □ C[n + 2]).Adj (a, b) (c, d) ↔ (↑a + 1 = ↑c ∨ ↑c + 1 = ↑a) ∧ b = d ∨ (b - d = 1 ∨ d - b = 1) ∧ a = c All goals completed! 🐙

3.3.3. Sum and Sigma Graphs*🔗

Given graphs G : SimpleGraph V and H : SimpleGraph W, their (disjoint) sum G ⊕g H is the graph formed by placing a copy of G and a copy of H side by side, with no edges between them. Its vertex type is the sum type V ⊕ W, whose elements are either Sum.inl v with v : V or Sum.inr w with w : W. Two vertices Sum.inl v₁ and Sum.inl v₂ are adjacent iff G.Adj v₁ v₂, two vertices Sum.inr w₁ and Sum.inr w₂ are adjacent iff H.Adj w₁ w₂, and no vertex Sum.inl v is adjacent to any vertex Sum.inr w. Mathlib defines G ⊕g H by pattern matching on these cases.

@[simps!] protected def sum (G : SimpleGraph V) (H : SimpleGraph W) : SimpleGraph (V ⊕ W) where Adj | Sum.inl u, Sum.inl v => G.Adj u v | Sum.inr u, Sum.inr v => H.Adj u v | _, _ => false symm.symm | Sum.inl u, Sum.inl v => G.adj_symm | Sum.inr u, Sum.inr v => H.adj_symm | Sum.inl _, Sum.inr _ | Sum.inr _, Sum.inl _ => id#source SimpleGraph.sum SimpleGraph.sum_adj_inl.{u_3, u_5} {V : Type u_3} {W : Type u_5} {G : SimpleGraph V} {H : SimpleGraph W} {v v' : V} : (G ⊕g H).Adj (Sum.inl v) (Sum.inl v') ↔ G.Adj v v'#check sum_adj_inl SimpleGraph.sum_adj_inr.{u_3, u_5} {V : Type u_3} {W : Type u_5} {G : SimpleGraph V} {H : SimpleGraph W} {w w' : W} : (G ⊕g H).Adj (Sum.inr w) (Sum.inr w') ↔ H.Adj w w'#check sum_adj_inr

More generally, we can take the disjoint union of an indexed family of graphs, which we call a sigma graph. This is not currently in Mathlib, so we define it here. If the graph indexed by i : ι has vertex type V i, then the vertex type of the disjoint union is the dependent pair (or Sigma) type Σ i, V i.

@[pp_using_anonymous_constructor] structure Sigma {α : Type u} (β : α → Type v) where /-- Constructs a dependent pair. Using this constructor in a context in which the type is not known usually requires a type ascription to determine `β`. This is because the desired relationship between the two values can't generally be determined automatically. -/ mk :: /-- The first component of a dependent pair. -/ fst : α /-- The second component of a dependent pair. Its type depends on the first component. -/ snd : β fst#source Sigma

A vertex of Σ i, V i is a pair ⟨i, u⟩ consisting of an index i : ι and an element u : V i. The pair is called dependent because the type of its second component depends on the value of its first. Lean prints Σ i, V i as (i : ι) × V i, so expect to see that form in goals and #check output.

Two vertices ⟨i, u⟩ and ⟨j, v⟩ should be adjacent iff i = j and u and v are adjacent in G i. Stating this takes some care: u : V i but v : V j, so (G i).Adj u v does not typecheck. A proof h : i = j does not fix this on its own, because Lean only identifies types that are equal by definition, and V i and V j are not. Instead we use h to transport v along the equation, giving h ▸ v : V i.

We mark the definition protected, so that even inside namespace SimpleGraph it must be called SimpleGraph.sigma (or Σg). This stops the short name sigma from clashing with other functions of that name, such as Finset.sigma.

/-- The disjoint union of an indexed family of graphs. Given an index type ι and, for each i : ι, a graph G i on the vertex type V i, the disjoint union Σg G has vertex type Σ i, V i, and two vertices are adjacent iff they lie in the same graph G i and are adjacent there. -/ @[simps!] protected def sigma {ι : Type*} {V : ι → Type*} (G : (i : ι) → SimpleGraph (V i)) : SimpleGraph (Σ i, V i) where Adj := fun ⟨i, u⟩ ⟨j, v⟩ => ∃ h : i = j, (G i).Adj u (h ▸ v) symm := V✝:Type u_1ι:Type u_2V:ι → Type u_3G:(i : ι) → SimpleGraph (V i)⊢ Std.Symm fun x x_1 ↦ match x with | ⟨i, u⟩ => match x_1 with | ⟨j, v⟩ => ∃ (h : i = j), (G i).Adj u (⋯ ▸ v) V✝:Type u_1ι:Type u_2V:ι → Type u_3G:(i : ι) → SimpleGraph (V i)⊢ ∀ (a b : (i : ι) × V i), (match a with | ⟨i, u⟩ => match b with | ⟨j, v⟩ => ∃ (h : i = j), (G i).Adj u (⋯ ▸ v)) → match b with | ⟨i, u⟩ => match a with | ⟨j, v⟩ => ∃ (h : i = j), (G i).Adj u (⋯ ▸ v) V✝:Type u_1ι:Type u_2V:ι → Type u_3G:(i : ι) → SimpleGraph (V i)i:ιu:V iv:V ihadj:(G i).Adj u (⋯ ▸ v)⊢ match ⟨i, v⟩ with | ⟨i_1, u_1⟩ => match ⟨i, u⟩ with | ⟨j, v⟩ => ∃ (h : i_1 = j), (G i_1).Adj u_1 (⋯ ▸ v) All goals completed! 🐙

In the proof of symm above, rintro ⟨i, u⟩ ⟨j, v⟩ ⟨rfl, hadj⟩ introduces the two vertices and splits the adjacency proof into its two parts. The pattern rfl substitutes i = j everywhere, after which h ▸ v reduces to v.

The substitution is needed because the cast h ▸ v only computes (in the sense of Definitional And Propositional Equalities) when both sides of h are definitionally equal, in which case it reduces to v. While i and j are distinct variables the cast is stuck, just like 0 + n, and no amount of unfolding gets past it to v. We will meet stuck casts again when we decide adjacency in Decidability And Kernel Reduction and when we change the endpoints of walks in Copy.

The @[simps!] attribute generates sigma_adj, in which the ⋯ hides the proof of i = j used by ▸. We write Σg G for SimpleGraph.sigma G.

SimpleGraph.sigma_adj.{u_2, u_3} {ι : Type u_2} {V : ι → Type u_3} (G : (i : ι) → SimpleGraph (V i)) (x✝ x✝¹ : (i : ι) × V i) : (SimpleGraph.sigma G).Adj x✝ x✝¹ = ∃ (h : x✝.fst = x✝¹.fst), (G x✝.fst).Adj x✝.snd (⋯ ▸ x✝¹.snd)#check SimpleGraph.sigma_adj @[inherit_doc] scoped prefix:60 "Σg " => SimpleGraph.sigma /-- The disjoint union of the complete graphs K[0], K[1], K[2], …. -/ abbrev natDisjointComplete : SimpleGraph (Σ i, Fin i) := Σg (fun (i : ℕ) => K[i])

Two vertices ⟨i, a⟩ and ⟨j, b⟩ of this graph are adjacent iff they lie in the same complete graph (i = j) and are distinct. We cannot write a ≠ b here, since a : Fin i and b : Fin j have different types; this is the same problem as above. Comparing the underlying natural numbers (a : ℕ) and (b : ℕ) avoids it.

In the proof, t₁ <;> t₂ runs the tactic t₂ on every goal produced by t₁: here constructor splits the ↔ into two implications, and rintro ⟨rfl, h⟩ then introduces the hypotheses in both, substituting as in the sigma proof above.

example {i j : ℕ} {a : Fin i} {b : Fin j} : natDisjointComplete.Adj ⟨i, a⟩ ⟨j, b⟩ ↔ i = j ∧ (a : ℕ) ≠ b := V:Type u_1i:ℕj:ℕa:Fin ib:Fin j⊢ natDisjointComplete.Adj ⟨i, a⟩ ⟨j, b⟩ ↔ i = j ∧ ↑a ≠ ↑b V:Type u_1i:ℕj:ℕa:Fin ib:Fin j⊢ natDisjointComplete.Adj ⟨i, a⟩ ⟨j, b⟩ → i = j ∧ ↑a ≠ ↑bV:Type u_1i:ℕj:ℕa:Fin ib:Fin j⊢ i = j ∧ ↑a ≠ ↑b → natDisjointComplete.Adj ⟨i, a⟩ ⟨j, b⟩ V:Type u_1i:ℕj:ℕa:Fin ib:Fin j⊢ natDisjointComplete.Adj ⟨i, a⟩ ⟨j, b⟩ → i = j ∧ ↑a ≠ ↑bV:Type u_1i:ℕj:ℕa:Fin ib:Fin j⊢ i = j ∧ ↑a ≠ ↑b → natDisjointComplete.Adj ⟨i, a⟩ ⟨j, b⟩ V:Type u_1i:ℕa:Fin ib:Fin ih:↑a ≠ ↑b⊢ natDisjointComplete.Adj ⟨i, a⟩ ⟨i, b⟩ V:Type u_1i:ℕa:Fin ib:Fin ih:((fun i ↦ K[i]) i).Adj a (⋯ ▸ b)⊢ i = i ∧ ↑a ≠ ↑b All goals completed! 🐙 V:Type u_1i:ℕa:Fin ib:Fin ih:↑a ≠ ↑b⊢ natDisjointComplete.Adj ⟨i, a⟩ ⟨i, b⟩ All goals completed! 🐙

3.4. Hypercube🔗

Often there is more than one way to construct a particular graph. A good example of this is the n-dimensional hypercube, which can be constructed in many different ways: as the Hasse diagram of the Boolean algebra of subsets of an n-element set; as the graph on Fin n → Bool with edges between vertices that differ in exactly one coordinate (i.e. at Hamming distance one); or as the box product of n copies of K₂.

The Hasse diagram construction is very easy to give, but then is a pain to work with.

/-- The Hasse diagram construction of the n-dimensional hypercube. -/ abbrev hypercubeHasse (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Finset (Fin n)) := hasse _

The Hamming graph construction is also easy to give and easier to work with than the Hasse diagram.

/-- The Hamming graph definition of the n-dimensional hypercube. -/ def hypercubeHamming (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin n → Bool) where Adj x y := hammingDist x y = 1 symm := V:Type u_1n:ℕ⊢ Std.Symm fun x y ↦ hammingDist x y = 1 V:Type u_1n:ℕ⊢ ∀ (a b : Fin n → Bool), hammingDist a b = 1 → hammingDist b a = 1; All goals completed! 🐙

But for our purposes the most useful construction of the hypercube is as the box product of n copies of K₂.

The box product construction of the hypercube requires a bit more setup, but will be worth it. The reason we choose this construction is that it is recursive in n: its vertex type is built so that Q[n + 1] = Q[n] □ K₂ holds definitionally. Almost every result we prove about the hypercube in the later chapters is by induction on n, and this recursive structure is exactly what allows these to work. It also lets us reuse Mathlib's box product lemmas directly.

For the box product construction we need to first define the vertex type of the hypercube. There are two things we need to decide: firstly what should the vertex type of Q[0] be? Since Q[0] is a single vertex we will use the canonical type with exactly one element, Unit.

Unit : Type#check Unit

Second when we said Q[n + 1] = Q[n] □ K₂ we need to choose a vertex type for K₂. We will choose the type Bool with its two elements, false and true.

inductive Bool : Type where /-- The Boolean value `false`, not to be confused with the proposition `False`. -/ | false : Bool /-- The Boolean value `true`, not to be confused with the proposition `True`. -/ | true : Bool#source Bool /-- The vertex type of the n-dimensional hypercube (box-product construction). -/ @[implicit_reducible] def HypercubeVert : ℕ → Type | 0 => Unit -- The canonical type with exactly one element | n + 1 => HypercubeVert n × Bool -- The previous vertex type times Bool

(Note that HypercubeVert n is really just Bool ^ n but defined so that the recursion holds definitionally. We can still easily take the Hamming distance viewpoint and we will equip it with the Hamming distance when needed in Hamming Paths.)

The @[implicit_reducible] attribute lets Lean unfold HypercubeVert (n + 1) to HypercubeVert n × Bool when it checks that implicit arguments have the expected type (as simp does before rewriting), while keeping HypercubeVert opaque to instance search so that the instances we provide for HypercubeVert n below are still found.

@[simp] lemma hypercubeVert_zero : HypercubeVert 0 = Unit := rfl lemma hypercubeVert_succ (n : ℕ) : HypercubeVert (n + 1) = (HypercubeVert n × Bool) := rfl

The n-dimensional hypercube can now be defined recursively as the box product of the previous hypercube with K₂, the complete graph on two vertices (where Bool is the vertex type of K₂).

/-- The n-dimensional hypercube defined as the box product of n copies of K₂. -/ def hypercube : (n : ℕ) → SimpleGraph (HypercubeVert n) -- The empty graph on one vertex | 0 => ⊥ -- The box product of the n-hypercube with K₂ on Bool | n + 1 => (hypercube n).boxProd ⊤ @[simp] lemma hypercube_zero : hypercube 0 = ⊥ := rfl lemma hypercube_succ (n : ℕ) : hypercube (n + 1) = (hypercube n).boxProd ⊤ := rfl

We will use Q[n] as notation for the n-dimensional hypercube.

@[inherit_doc hypercube] scoped notation "Q[" n "]" => hypercube n

Adjacency in Q[n + 1] is characterized recursively: two vertices are adjacent iff they agree in the last coordinate and are adjacent in Q[n], or they differ in the last coordinate and agree everywhere else. This holds by rfl (it is boxProd_adj with the second graph ⊤), and marking it @[simp] lets simp decide adjacency in the hypercube recursively. (For the base case simp can already chain hypercube_zero with bot_adj.)

@[simp] lemma hypercube_succ_adj {n : ℕ} {u v : HypercubeVert (n + 1)} : Q[n + 1].Adj u v ↔ (Q[n].Adj u.1 v.1 ∧ u.2 = v.2) ∨ (u.2 ≠ v.2 ∧ u.1 = v.1) := Iff.rfl

3.5. Mycielskian🔗

The Mycielskian of a graph G : SimpleGraph V is constructed as follows. Its vertex set consists of two disjoint copies Vₗ and Vᵣ of V together with a new vertex none.

The edges inside Vₗ are identical to those of G; there are no edges inside Vᵣ; there is an edge between vertices a ∈ Vₗ and b ∈ Vᵣ iff there is an edge in G between the vertices of which a and b are copies. Finally none is adjacent to every vertex in Vᵣ but to no vertices in Vₗ.

This construction is due to Jan Mycielski,J. Mycielski, Sur le coloriage des graphes, Colloquium Mathematicum 3 (1955), 161–162. who showed that:

  1. if G is triangle-free, then mμ[G] is also triangle-free.

  2. if G has chromatic number k, then mμ[G] has chromatic number k + 1.

Thus starting with any triangle-free graph we can use it to construct triangle-free graphs with arbitrarily large chromatic number.

In order to define the Mycielskian of a graph G in Lean we need to first describe its vertex type. Given that it is built from two disjoint copies of the vertex type of G together with a new vertex, we can use Option (V ⊕ V). (We already saw the Sum type ⊕ for completeBipartiteGraph and Option is the natural way to extend a type with a new element called none.)

@[suggest_for Maybe, suggest_for Optional, suggest_for Nullable] inductive Option (α : Type u) where /-- No value. -/ | none : Option α /-- Some value of type `α`. -/ | some (val : α) : Option α#source Option /-- The *Mycielskian* of a graph G. -/ @[simps] def mycielskian (G : SimpleGraph V) : SimpleGraph (Option (V ⊕ V)) where Adj x y := match x, y with | some (Sum.inl v), some (Sum.inl w) => G.Adj v w | some (Sum.inl v), some (Sum.inr w) => G.Adj v w | some (Sum.inr v), some (Sum.inl w) => G.Adj v w | none , some (Sum.inr w) => True | some (Sum.inr v), none => True | _, _ => False symm We introduce the notation mμ[G] for the Mycielskian of a graph G.

@[inherit_doc mycielskian] scoped notation "mμ[" G "]" => mycielskian G

As mentioned above if we iterate the Mycielskian construction starting with a triangle-free graph then we obtain a sequence of triangle-free graphs with increasing chromatic number.

In particular we can start with the 5-cycle C[5], in which case the second graph in this sequence is called the Grötzsch graph.

/-- The *Grötzsch graph* (i.e. the Mycielskian of C[5]). -/ @[simps!] abbrev grotzschGraph : SimpleGraph (Option (Fin 5 ⊕ Fin 5)) := mμ[C[5]] SimpleGraph.grotzschGraph_adj (x y : Option (Fin 5 ⊕ Fin 5)) : grotzschGraph.Adj x y = match x, y with | some (Sum.inl v), some (Sum.inl w) => C[5].Adj v w | some (Sum.inl v), some (Sum.inr w) => C[5].Adj v w | some (Sum.inr v), some (Sum.inl w) => C[5].Adj v w | none, some (Sum.inr w) => True | some (Sum.inr w), none => True | x, x_1 => False#check grotzschGraph_adj

In order to talk about the vertices of mμ[G] it will be useful to introduce some terminology. We name the two copies of V in a mycielskian namespace, since these names only make sense for this construction.

/-- A copy of the vertex v in the "left" part of the Mycielskian. -/ abbrev left {V : Type*} (v : V) : Option (V ⊕ V) := some (Sum.inl v) /-- A copy of the vertex v in the "right" part of the Mycielskian. -/ abbrev right {V : Type*} (v : V) : Option (V ⊕ V) := some (Sum.inr v)

We can introduce notation for these as follows. The left copy of v : V is denoted v ₗ and the right copy is denoted v ᵣ.

@[inherit_doc mycielskian.left] scoped postfix:max "ₗ" => mycielskian.left @[inherit_doc mycielskian.right] scoped postfix:max "ᵣ" => mycielskian.right

The adjacency relation of mμ[G] between the named vertices v ₗ, v ᵣ and none is characterized by the following @[simp] lemmas. Each holds by rfl (the adjacency match reduces once the vertices are in constructor form), and together they let simp (and tactics such as aesop that call it) determine any adjacency in the Mycielskian.

@[simp] lemma mycielskian_adj_left_left {G : SimpleGraph V} (v w : V) : mμ[G].Adj (v ₗ) (w ₗ) ↔ G.Adj v w := Iff.rfl @[simp] lemma mycielskian_adj_left_right {G : SimpleGraph V} (v w : V) : mμ[G].Adj (v ₗ) (w ᵣ) ↔ G.Adj v w := Iff.rfl @[simp] lemma mycielskian_adj_right_left {G : SimpleGraph V} (v w : V) : mμ[G].Adj (v ᵣ) (w ₗ) ↔ G.Adj v w := Iff.rfl @[simp] lemma mycielskian_adj_right_right {G : SimpleGraph V} (v w : V) : ¬ mμ[G].Adj (v ᵣ) (w ᵣ) := fun h => h @[simp] lemma mycielskian_adj_none_right {G : SimpleGraph V} (w : V) : mμ[G].Adj none (w ᵣ) := trivial @[simp] lemma mycielskian_adj_right_none {G : SimpleGraph V} (v : V) : mμ[G].Adj (v ᵣ) none := trivial @[simp] lemma mycielskian_adj_left_none {G : SimpleGraph V} (v : V) : ¬ mμ[G].Adj (v ₗ) none := fun h => h @[simp] lemma mycielskian_adj_none_left {G : SimpleGraph V} (w : V) : ¬ mμ[G].Adj none (w ₗ) := fun h => h

We now prove a few lemmas about the Mycielskian construction that will be useful later on.

The maps v ↦ v ₗ and v ↦ v ᵣ are injective. (In the proofs, e |>.comp f means (e).comp f: the |>. lets us use dot notation on the result of Option.some_injective _ without extra brackets.)

lemma mycielskian.left_injective {V : Type*} : Function.Injective (fun v : V => v ₗ) := Option.some_injective _ |>.comp Sum.inl_injective lemma mycielskian.right_injective {V : Type*} : Function.Injective (fun v : V => v ᵣ) := Option.some_injective _ |>.comp Sum.inr_injective

The neighbourhoods of the vertices in mμ[G] are as follows.

v ₗ is adjacent to the left and right copies of the neighbours of v in G.

@[simp] lemma mycielskian_neighborSet_left {G : SimpleGraph V} (v : V) : mμ[G].neighborSet (v ₗ) = (G.neighborSet v).image (· ₗ) ∪ (G.neighborSet v).image (· ᵣ) := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vv:V⊢ mμ[G].neighborSet v ₗ = (fun x ↦ x ₗ) '' G.neighborSet v ∪ (fun x ↦ x ᵣ) '' G.neighborSet v V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vv:Vx:Option (V ⊕ V)⊢ x ∈ mμ[G].neighborSet v ₗ ↔ x ∈ (fun x ↦ x ₗ) '' G.neighborSet v ∪ (fun x ↦ x ᵣ) '' G.neighborSet v All goals completed! 🐙

v ᵣ is adjacent to the left copies of the neighbours of v in G and to none.

@[simp] lemma mycielskian_neighborSet_right {G : SimpleGraph V} (v : V) : mμ[G].neighborSet (v ᵣ) = insert none ((G.neighborSet v).image (· ₗ)) := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vv:V⊢ mμ[G].neighborSet v ᵣ = insert none ((fun x ↦ x ₗ) '' G.neighborSet v) V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vv:Vx:Option (V ⊕ V)⊢ x ∈ mμ[G].neighborSet v ᵣ ↔ x ∈ insert none ((fun x ↦ x ₗ) '' G.neighborSet v) All goals completed! 🐙

none is adjacent to the right copies of all vertices in G.

@[simp] lemma mycielskian_neighborSet_none {G : SimpleGraph V} : mμ[G].neighborSet none = Set.range (· ᵣ) := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph V⊢ mμ[G].neighborSet none = Set.range fun x ↦ x ᵣ V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vx:Option (V ⊕ V)⊢ x ∈ mμ[G].neighborSet none ↔ x ∈ Set.range fun x ↦ x ᵣ All goals completed! 🐙

The left copies, the right copies and none are pairwise disjoint.

@[simp] lemma mycielskian.disjoint_image_left_image_right (s t : Set V) : Disjoint (s.image (· ₗ)) (t.image (· ᵣ)) := V:Type u_1s:Set Vt:Set V⊢ Disjoint ((fun x ↦ x ₗ) '' s) ((fun x ↦ x ᵣ) '' t) All goals completed! 🐙 @[simp] lemma mycielskian.disjoint_image_left_none (s : Set V) : Disjoint (s.image (· ₗ)) {none} := V:Type u_1s:Set V⊢ Disjoint ((fun x ↦ x ₗ) '' s) {none} All goals completed! 🐙 @[simp] lemma mycielskian.disjoint_image_right_none (s : Set V) : Disjoint (s.image (· ᵣ)) {none} := V:Type u_1s:Set V⊢ Disjoint ((fun x ↦ x ᵣ) '' s) {none} All goals completed! 🐙

As mentioned above we will be interested in iterating the Mycielskian construction, but in order to do this we first need to define the iterated vertex type.Below we use Type _ which means that the universe level is inferred (it will be the same as the universe level of V). If you replace Type _ with Type* the definition would need to change.

As with HypercubeVert, the @[implicit_reducible] attribute lets Lean unfold mμᵥ^(n + 1) V when checking implicit and instance-implicit arguments.

/-- The vertex type of the n-th Mycielskian of a SimpleGraph V (denoted mμᵥ^n V). -/ @[implicit_reducible] def MycielskianVert (V : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ | 0 => V | n + 1 => Option (MycielskianVert V n ⊕ MycielskianVert V n) @[simp] lemma mycielskianVert_zero {V : Type*} : MycielskianVert V 0 = V := rfl lemma mycielskianVert_succ {V : Type*} (n : ℕ) : MycielskianVert V (n + 1) = Option (MycielskianVert V n ⊕ MycielskianVert V n) := rfl

Notation for the vertex type of the n-th Mycielskian.

@[inherit_doc MycielskianVert] scoped syntax "mμᵥ^" term:max term:max : term scoped macro_rules | `(mμᵥ^ $n $V) => `(MycielskianVert $V $n) /-- The n-th iterated Mycielskian of a graph G (denoted mμ^n G). -/ def iterMycielskian {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : (n : ℕ) → SimpleGraph (mμᵥ^n V) | 0 => G | n + 1 => mμ[iterMycielskian G n] @[simp] lemma iterMycielskian_zero {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : iterMycielskian G 0 = G := rfl lemma iterMycielskian_succ {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) (n : ℕ) : iterMycielskian G (n + 1) = mμ[iterMycielskian G n] := rfl

Notation for the iterated Mycielskian:

@[inherit_doc iterMycielskian] scoped syntax "mμ^" term:max term:max : term scoped macro_rules | `(mμ^ $n $G) => `(iterMycielskian $G $n) C[5].iterMycielskian 3 : SimpleGraph (MycielskianVert (Fin 5) 3)#check mμ^3 C[5]

The postfixes ₗ and ᵣ can be stacked: (0 : Fin 5)ₗᵣᵣ means ((0ₗ)ᵣ)ᵣ, the right copy of the right copy of the left copy of 0, which is a vertex of the 3rd iterated Mycielskian of C[5]. Written out in full this would be the unreadable term some (Sum.inr (some (Sum.inr (some (Sum.inl 0))))). The adjacency lemmas above peel off one layer at a time: left–left and right–left pairs are adjacent exactly when the underlying vertices are, so (0 : Fin 5)ₗᵣᵣ is adjacent to (1 : Fin 5)ₗₗₗ because 0 and 1 are adjacent in C[5].

example : (mμ^3 C[5]).Adj (0 : Fin 5)ₗᵣᵣ (1 : Fin 5)ₗₗₗ := V:Type u_1⊢ (C[5].iterMycielskian 3).Adj 0ₗᵣᵣ 1ₗₗₗ simpa [iterMycielskian_succ] using (V:Type u_1⊢ C[5].Adj 0 1 All goals completed! 🐙 : C[5].Adj 0 1)

3.6. Complete Multipartite Graphs and Blow-ups*🔗

Having earlier introduced complete bipartite graphs we would now like to discuss complete multipartite graphs and their generalization blow-up graphs. However these constructions make use of the SimpleGraph.comap construction which we won't formally introduce until Comaps. In order to properly understand these constructions you may wish to read that short section now.

3.6.1. Complete Multipartite Graphs🔗

A complete multipartite graph is a graph in which the vertices are partitioned into classes so that two vertices are adjacent if and only if they are in different classes. The definition in Mathlib looks rather forbidding at first glance:

abbrev completeMultipartiteGraph {ι : Type*} (V : ι → Type*) : SimpleGraph (Σ i, V i) := .comap Sigma.fst ⊤#source completeMultipartiteGraph -- (V : ι → Type*) : SimpleGraph (Σ i, V i) -- := SimpleGraph.comap Sigma.fst ⊤ lemma completeMultipartiteGraph_adj {ι : Type*} (V : ι → Type*) (u v : Σ i, V i) : (completeMultipartiteGraph V).Adj u v ↔ u.fst ≠ v.fst := Iff.rfl

This will make more sense once we see Comaps, but we can already try to parse it.

We start with an index type ι (the labels of the vertex classes) and a function V : ι → Type*. The vertex type of the graph is Σ i, V i, the dependent pair or Sigma type that we met in Sum And Sigma Graphs.

@[pp_using_anonymous_constructor] structure Sigma {α : Type u} (β : α → Type v) where /-- Constructs a dependent pair. Using this constructor in a context in which the type is not known usually requires a type ascription to determine `β`. This is because the desired relationship between the two values can't generally be determined automatically. -/ mk :: /-- The first component of a dependent pair. -/ fst : α /-- The second component of a dependent pair. Its type depends on the first component. -/ snd : β fst#source Sigma

Recall that a vertex v : Σ i, V i is a pair ⟨i, w⟩ consisting of an index i : ι and an element w : V i; the class labelled by i is then the set of vertices whose first component is i.

The Sigma type plays the same role here that the Sum type played for complete bipartite graphs. Just as a vertex of a sum type knows which of the two sides it came from, since it is either a Sum.inl or a Sum.inr, a vertex of Σ i, V i knows which class it lies in, since it carries its index. The two alternatives inl and inr have simply been replaced by one alternative for each i : ι.

Sigma.fst.{u, v} {α : Type u} {β : α → Type v} (self : Sigma β) : α#check Sigma.fst -- The first component of a dependent pair ⟨i, w⟩.

The SimpleGraph.comap then defines edges in the graph by pulling back the adjacency relation from ⊤ : SimpleGraph ι, the complete graph on ι, using Sigma.fst. So vertices are adjacent if and only if their first components are different.

protected def comap (f : V → W) (G : SimpleGraph W) : SimpleGraph V where Adj u v := G.Adj (f u) (f v) symm.symm _ _ h := h.symm#source SimpleGraph.comap

For example, the complete multipartite graph with n classes, where each class is a copy of ℕ can be defined as follows:

/-- The complete multipartite graph with n classes, where each class is a copy of ℕ. -/ @[simps!] abbrev multiNat (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Σ _ : Fin n, ℕ) := completeMultipartiteGraph fun (_ : Fin n) => ℕ SimpleGraph.multiNat_adj (n : ℕ) (u v : (i : Fin n) × (fun x ↦ ℕ) i) : (multiNat n).Adj u v = ¬u.fst = v.fst#check multiNat_adj -- produced by the @[simps!] attribute on multiNat

We can also define the complete multipartite graph with classes indexed by ℕ, where the n-th class is Fin n.

/-- The complete multipartite graph with classes indexed by ℕ, where the n-th class is Fin n -/ @[simps!] abbrev natFinMulti : SimpleGraph (Σ n : ℕ, Fin n) := completeMultipartiteGraph (fun n => Fin n) SimpleGraph.natFinMulti_adj (u v : (i : ℕ) × (fun n ↦ Fin n) i) : natFinMulti.Adj u v = ¬u.fst = v.fst#check natFinMulti_adj

Deciding whether two vertices are adjacent in a complete multipartite graph is easy: they are adjacent if and only if their first components are different. So decidability of adjacency follows from decidability of equality on their index type. Since Fin n and ℕ have decidable equality so multiNat and natFinMulti have decidable adjacency.

example : (multiNat 3).Adj ⟨0, 12⟩ ⟨2, 10⟩ := V:Type u_1⊢ (multiNat 3).Adj ⟨0, 12⟩ ⟨2, 10⟩ All goals completed! 🐙 example : ¬ natFinMulti.Adj ⟨3, 0⟩ ⟨3, 1⟩ := V:Type u_1⊢ ¬natFinMulti.Adj ⟨3, 0⟩ ⟨3, 1⟩ All goals completed! 🐙

3.6.2. Blow-ups🔗

While not currently in Mathlib we can define the blow-up of a graph G by replacing each vertex with a class of vertices and defining edges between vertices in different classes according to the edges in G. (This is a trivial generalization of the completeMultipartiteGraph construction, which is the special case where G is a complete graph.)

/-- The blow-up of a graph G given by replacing each vertex i with a class of vertices V i -/ @[simps!] abbrev blowUpGraph {ι : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph ι) (V : ι → Type*) : SimpleGraph (Σ i, V i) := SimpleGraph.comap Sigma.fst G SimpleGraph.blowUpGraph_adj.{u_2, u_3} {ι : Type u_2} (G : SimpleGraph ι) (V : ι → Type u_3) (u v : (i : ι) × V i) : (G.blowUpGraph V).Adj u v = G.Adj u.fst v.fst#check blowUpGraph_adj -- (G.blowUpGraph V).Adj u v = G.Adj u.fst v.fst

The n-uniform blow-up of a graph G is the blow-up of G where each vertex is replaced by a class of size n.

/-- The n-uniform blow-up of a graph G given by replacing each vertex i with n vertices (Fin n) denoted G[n] -/ @[simps!] abbrev blowUpN {ι : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph ι) (n : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Σ _ : ι, Fin n) := G.blowUpGraph (fun _ => Fin n)

We can introduce notation G[n] for the n-uniform blow-up of G as follows:

@[inherit_doc blowUpN] scoped notation:max G "[" n "]" => blowUpN G n C[4][3] : SimpleGraph ((_ : Fin 4) × Fin 3)#check C[4][3] -- the blow-up of C[4] replacing each vertex with a class of size 3 example : C[4][3].Adj ⟨1, 2⟩ ⟨2, 0⟩ := V:Type u_1⊢ C[4][3].Adj ⟨1, 2⟩ ⟨2, 0⟩ All goals completed! 🐙 example : ¬ C[4][3].Adj ⟨0, 0⟩ ⟨2, 1⟩ := V:Type u_1⊢ ¬C[4][3].Adj ⟨0, 0⟩ ⟨2, 1⟩ All goals completed! 🐙

3.7. Kneser Graphs*🔗

The k-th Kneser graph on a type β has as vertices the k-element subsets of β, with edges between any distinct disjoint subsets. Before we can define this as a SimpleGraph we need to decide what the vertex type should be. If we are happy to work with finite types (i.e. to assume Fintype β) then we could use (Finset.univ : Finset β).powersetCard k which is the finite family of k-element subsets of a finite type β.

Finset.powersetCard.{u_1} {α : Type u_1} (n : ℕ) (s : Finset α) : Finset (Finset α)#check Finset.powersetCard

Using Finset.powersetCard gives us easy access to lots of counting results about families of finite sets, which would be useful. However this is a term not a type so if we define a SimpleGraph on this then Lean will coerce this to a type and our Kneser graph vertices will have type: ↥((Finset.univ : Finset β).powersetCard k). This is possible, but a bit awkward.

The second option is to use the subtype of Finset β consisting of k-element subsets, i.e. {s : Finset β // s.card = k}. This means we no longer need to assume Fintype β but we lose direct access to the Finset.powersetCard results. However we can solve this issue with a simple translation lemma saying that, for any predicate p, counting the k-element subsets satisfying p as terms of the subtype {s : Finset β // s.card = k} gives the same answer as counting them as members of the family (Finset.univ : Finset β).powersetCard k. (See Independence Number Of The Kneser Graph for details.)

/-- The k-th Kneser graph on β: vertices are k-element subsets of β, and edges join disjoint, distinct subsets. -/ @[simps] def kneserGraph (β : Type*) (k : ℕ) : SimpleGraph {s : Finset β // s.card = k} where Adj u v := Disjoint u.val v.val ∧ u ≠ v symm := ⟨fun _ _ h => ⟨h.1.symm, h.2.symm⟩⟩ loopless := ⟨fun _ h => h.2 rfl⟩ instance (β : Type*) (k : ℕ) [DecidableEq β] : DecidableRel ((kneserGraph β k).Adj) := fun u v => V:Type u_1β:Type u_2k:ℕinst✝:DecidableEq βu:{ s // s.card = k }v:{ s // s.card = k }⊢ Decidable ((kneserGraph β k).Adj u v) V:Type u_1β:Type u_2k:ℕinst✝:DecidableEq βu:{ s // s.card = k }v:{ s // s.card = k }⊢ Decidable ({ Adj := fun u v ↦ Disjoint ↑u ↑v ∧ u ≠ v, symm := ⋯, loopless := ⋯ }.Adj u v); All goals completed! 🐙 /-- The k-th Kneser graph on Fin n: vertices are k-element subsets of Fin n, and edges join disjoint, distinct subsets. -/ scoped notation "Kn[" n ", " k "]" => kneserGraph (Fin n) k

A special case of the Kneser graph is the Petersen graph, which is Kn[5, 2].

/-- The *Petersen* graph which is the Kneser graph Kn[5, 2]. -/ abbrev petersenGraph : SimpleGraph {s : Finset (Fin 5) // s.card = 2} := Kn[5, 2] SimpleGraph.kneserGraph_adj.{u_2} (β : Type u_2) (k : ℕ) (u v : { s // s.card = k }) : (kneserGraph β k).Adj u v = (Disjoint ↑u ↑v ∧ u ≠ v)#check kneserGraph_adj -- (kneserGraph β k).Adj u v ↔ Disjoint ↑u ↑v ∧ u ≠ v

We will look at the independence number of Kn[n, k] in Cliques and colourings of Kn[n, k] in Exercises Colorings. Computing its independence number is really just a case of translating the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem (which is in Mathlib) into the language of SimpleGraph.

After ext the goal mentions a new variable of type ZMod 17, but decide only works on statements with no free variables. Instead use decide +revert, which first reverts the variable and then checks the resulting statement ∀ y : ZMod 17, … case by case.

Solutions

  1. Show that a Cayley graph defined in a commutative additive group is simply a circulant graph.

example (G : Type*) [AddCommGroup G] (s : Set G) : addCayley s = circulantGraph s := G:Type u_1inst✝:AddCommGroup Gs:Set G⊢ addCayley s = circulantGraph s G:Type u_1inst✝:AddCommGroup Gs:Set Gu:Gv:G⊢ (addCayley s).Adj u v ↔ (circulantGraph s).Adj u v G:Type u_1inst✝:AddCommGroup Gs:Set Gu:Gv:G⊢ (u ≠ v ∧ ∃ g ∈ s, u + g = v ∨ u = v + g) ↔ ¬u = v ∧ (u - v ∈ s ∨ v - u ∈ s) All goals completed! 🐙

  1. Show that the Paley graph on 17 vertices is a circulant graph with the following differences.

lemma paleyGraph₁₇_eq_circulant : paleyGraph (ZMod 17) = circulantGraph ({1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 13, 15, 16}) := ⊢ paleyGraph (ZMod 17) = circulantGraph {1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 13, 15, 16} this:{y | IsSquare y} = {0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 13, 15, 16}⊢ paleyGraph (ZMod 17) = circulantGraph {1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 13, 15, 16} All goals completed! 🐙
